allies.rationale_text: Cognitive Load Theory helps the router choose simpler structures so complexity is processed without overload.
allies.source_quote: By routing complex ideas through simple organizational structures, concept maps, or analogies, the RMR ensures that new information is broken into absorbable chunks.
allies.affinity_rationale: Canonical: 'The RMR's goal is to minimize unnecessary cognitive load' — routes complex ideas through simple structures to maximize learning efficiency.
allies.activation_condition: When routing reasoning through appropriate modes requires managing cognitive load to avoid overwhelming working memory.

allies.rationale_text: Metacognitive reflection gives the router the self-monitoring needed to test whether the current mode is actually working.
allies.source_quote: Metacognition includes the planning aspect ("What are my goals?") and the monitoring aspect ("Could I learn this idea in a different way?").
allies.affinity_rationale: Canonical: 'This is the self-awareness required for effective routing' — metacognition enables planning ('What are my goals?') and monitoring ('Could I learn this differently?').
allies.activation_condition: When conscious awareness of one's own reasoning process is needed to select the most effective reasoning mode.

antagonists.rationale_text: Confirmation bias hijacks routing by pushing the problem-solving path toward defending a preferred conclusion.
antagonists.source_quote: This bypasses objective mode selection, forcing the problem-solving effort to defend a preconceived idea.
antagonists.affinity_rationale: Canonical: 'Motivated reasoning actively hijacks the RMR, forcing the problem-solving effort to defend a preconceived idea regardless of contradictory evidence.'
antagonists.activation_condition: When motivated reasoning hijacks mode selection to defend preconceived conclusions rather than genuinely discriminating problem structure.

antagonists.rationale_text: Commitment and consistency bias blocks route correction even when new evidence indicates another reasoning mode is needed.
antagonists.source_quote: This desire to avoid the "rigors of thinking" or the appearance of being inconsistent suppresses the RMR’s function to seek truth over comfort.
antagonists.affinity_rationale: Canonical: 'creates discomfort with inconsistency, leading people to stick with initial interpretations... suppresses the RMR's function to seek truth over comfort.'
antagonists.activation_condition: When the desire to appear consistent suppresses route correction even when new evidence indicates a different reasoning mode is needed.

structured_tensions.tension_text: Reasoning-mode-router conflicts with representativeness-heuristic when familiar labels force premature mode routing.
structured_tensions.source_quote: reasoning-mode-router conflicts with representativeness-heuristic when familiar labels force premature mode routing.

structured_tensions.tension_text: Reasoning-mode-router conflicts with anchoring when the first framing locks route selection despite contradictory evidence.
structured_tensions.source_quote: reasoning-mode-router conflicts with anchoring when first framing locks route selection despite contradictory evidence.

structured_tensions.tension_text: Reasoning-mode-router conflicts with confirmation-bias when the router is tuned to validate a preferred mode instead of the real problem structure.
structured_tensions.source_quote: reasoning-mode-router conflicts with confirmation-bias (confirmation bias) when routers are tuned to confirm preferred modes rather than genuinely discriminating problem structure.

structured_tensions.tension_text: Reasoning-mode-router conflicts with commitment-bias when discomfort with inconsistency suppresses route correction.
structured_tensions.source_quote: reasoning-mode-router conflicts with commitment-bias (commitment and consistency bias) when the discomfort of appearing inconsistent suppresses route correction even when new evidence indicates a different reasoning mode is needed.
